C1: for T1, T2, T3 and Y, cos(th) I + i sin(th) sigma equals the matrix exponential exp(i th sigma), is unitary, and gives (UH)^dag(UH) - H^dag H = 0 for any real theta and any complex H; this also holds in the physical normalisation exp(i alpha/2). C2: -I is unitary with det 1, equals both exp(i pi sigma3) and exp(2 pi i Y) with Y_H = 1/2, and maps (0, v/sqrt2) to (0, -v/sqrt2). S1: an explicit SU(2) element W(H) takes any H != 0 to (0, sqrt(H^dag H)), so SU(2) is transitive on each sphere. S2: the characteristic polynomial of M^2_ab = H^dag{t_a,t_b}H equals its value at (0, r) with r^2 = H^dag H; the eigenvalues at the vev are {g^2v^2/4 (x2), (g^2+g'^2)v^2/4, 0}. S3: the Z6 generator acts trivially on Q, u, d, L, e and H, while -I in SU(2) acts as -1 on H. S4 CONTROL: psi^dag H is invariant only when psi and H rotate together; it changes when H alone rotates. S5: the four generators span a rank-3 tangent space at the vev (the orbit is S^3); (I - sigma3)/2 moves the vev and Q = (I + sigma3)/2 annihilates it in tree normalisation. Separately, the tree's own excite.py --selftest (D19 rows, DOUBLET row, radial CONTROL) and --verify (V14 T1/T2/T3/Y residuals 0; '0 residual(s) not zero of 44') were run read-only and pass. git status of research/warp-drive is unchanged.

later_literature.what: Gauge-invariant (Froehlich-Morchio-Strocchi) formulation. The vev is gauge-dependent (gauges with <phi> = 0 exist). The minimum X = v alpha, with alpha an arbitrary SU(2) matrix, is a whole orbit invariant under gauge and custodial transformations. The physical spectrum is given by gauge-invariant composites. Confirms both claims and places them at tree level.

later_literature.ref: T. Cohen, N. Craig, X. Lu, D. Sutherland, 'Is SMEFT Enough?', arXiv:2008.08597v2 (2021)
later_literature.what: A doublet (SMEFT) description exists iff the scalar manifold has an O(4)-invariant point with analytic metric and potential. HEFT is required when a BSM state gets all its mass from EWSB or when there is extra EWSB. This narrows the doublet HYPOTHESIS to an empirical assumption, which the tree names; it does not narrow D19's conclusion. In either EFT, |H|^2 = (v0+h)^2/2 is the only zero-derivative O(4) building block.
Ongoing work to tell SMEFT from HEFT experimentally (positivity bounds, multi-Higgs amplitudes, di-Higgs). Only titles and abstracts were seen; none bears on the group identity.

audits.lacked_data: The result is an identity about a representation of the compact group SU(2)xU(1) on C^2: H^dag H is invariant under any unitary U, and -I lies in the group. No measured quantity enters it, so no datum the 1960s authors lacked can move it. It is re-derived here for every angle and every H (29/29). The only empirical content is the representation assignment, one doublet with Y = 1/2, and the tree names that as a hypothesis. Known now but not then: a 125 GeV scalar exists and behaves as the SM Higgs (Maas p.1, refs [8-11]). Still not settled: whether the scalar sector is linearly realised (SMEFT) or requires HEFT (Cohen et al. 2008.08597, READ). Evidence either way: if HEFT held, the doublet wording would need restating but D19's conclusion would not change, since h is a gauge singlet (Cohen eq. 2.8). If a second doublet existed, H1^dag H2 would be a physical relative orientation and D19 would not extend to it; the tree already lists 'a BSM light scalar' as unanswered (excite.py:280-288). For this result M's hypothesis is not supported: on the hypotheses the tree names, no missing datum changes the conclusion.
audits.grade_evidence: The statement is READ-VIA-RESTATEMENT in Maas 1712.04721 and Cohen et al. 2008.08597. Maas p.18-19: the minimum is phi^dag phi = f^2 and X = v alpha with alpha an arbitrary SU(2) matrix, 'manifestly invariant under ... gauge transformations'. Maas p.19: phi^dag phi is the only invariant. Cohen et al.: eq. 2.8. The symbolic re-derivation agrees for every theta and every complex H (C1). It exhibits -I in both SU(2) and U(1)_Y (C2), proves transitivity (S1), shows the mass eigenvalues depend on H only through H^dag H (S2), and shows the element mapping H -> -H survives the SM Z6 quotient (S3). The tree's own --selftest and --verify pass. No datum enters the conclusion. Three scope notes, none of which narrows the conclusion as used: (i) 'no derivative-free gauge-invariant local observable changes' needs 'of H alone, or with all fields transformed jointly'. A mixed invariant psi^dag H changes if H alone is moved (S4 CONTROL), while every mass is unchanged either way. (ii) The statement is tree level, which the tree does not name. (iii) It assumes a single doublet, which the tree does name. One discrepancy is recorded in the restating review: Maas footnote 13, 'G = SU(2)/Z2'. It is a loose footnote, refutes nothing, and is not repaired.
audits.what_would_change_the_grade: NARROWED if the tree, or a downstream owner of D19 such as specthm SR4, is found to apply 'no derivative-free gauge-invariant local observable changes' to a mixed composite (a Yukawa-type psi^dag H) while moving H alone at fixed fermions. Also NARROWED if D19 is extended to more than one scalar doublet or to a non-doublet scalar sector, or if the vev's direction is used at the quantum level without naming the tree-level hypothesis. WRONG only on a gauge-group element U and an H with (UH)^dag(UH) != H^dag H; the symbolic check excludes this for all four generators and all angles. DATA-DEPENDENT cannot be reached, because no measured quantity enters.

I could not refute the grade in either direction.

SOURCE READ. I read Maas arXiv:1712.04721v4 myself through alphaXiv (PDF pages 1, 4, 5, 7, 16, 20-22, 27, 32, 66). Every quotation in the audit matches the page text:
- p.2: "v ... is dependent on the gauge ... gauges ... in which <phi> = 0".
- p.18 eq. (35), phi^dag phi = f^2, and "X = v alpha, with ... alpha an arbitrary SU(2) matrix ... manifestly invariant under both, gauge transformations and custodial transformations".
- p.19: "the only group-invariant from which an invariant potential could be built is phi^dagger phi".
- p.63: "phi -> exp(i alpha(y)) phi under a hypercharge gauge transformation".
- Footnote 13 reads verbatim: "Actually, in the standard model G = SU(2)/Z2, due to the requirement of single-valuedness for the fermion fields [62]". p.29 says the same, and also gives SU(3)/Z3 for QCD.

The audit treats this footnote as a loose discrepancy in the restating review, not repaired and not quoted as an error in the journal version. That is correct and is not over-represented. Read literally, SU(2)/Z2 on its own could not act on any doublet, including H itself. Only a quotient of the product group by a diagonal centre subgroup acts trivially on every SM field. The image group acting on H is the same under any such quotient, so -I acting as -1 on H survives.

INDEPENDENT CHECKS. Script and output are in verify/refute/higgs_refute.py and higgs_refute.out; 5 of 5 pass.
- R1: a general SU(2)xU(1) element, exp(i th) times a ZYZ Euler product, preserves H^dag H symbolically for every complex H. This is the full group, not just the four one-parameter subgroups that V14 checks.
- R2: -I has det 1 and equals exp(i pi sigma3).
- R3 closes a gap in the audit's evidence. The audit says "every mass is unchanged", but its S2 checked only the gauge-boson mass matrix. I checked fermion masses numerically, using random complex 3x3 down- and up-type Yukawas with H~ = i sigma2 H*. When H alone is moved by a random SU(2)xU(1) element, the six quark singular values and a CKM commutator invariant are unchanged (max difference 8.9e-16). The reason is that the change can be absorbed by redefining Q, u_R and d_R.
- R4: the Higgs-sector Hessian spectrum of lam(|H|^2 - f^2/2)^2 is identical, {0 (x3), 2 f^2 lam}, at two different points of the vacuum orbit.
- R5 CONTROL: with two doublets, H1^dag H2 changes when only H2 is rotated. This confirms that the single-doublet boundary the audit names is real.

TREE RE-RUN. excite.py --selftest passed, read-only: the D19 T1/T2/T3/Y rows, the DOUBLET row and the radial CONTROL. The stored rederive output reads ALL PASS 29/29. Re-running the auditor's rederive script did not finish inside the 120 s tool timeout and was moved to the background. I never saw its output, so I have not re-run it myself; I rely on the stored result. git status of research/warp-drive shows only the pre-existing untracked docket67-raw/reverify/.

DOWNSTREAM USES. I checked every consumer of D19: specthm.py SR4 at lines 1385-1404, massform.py at 277-278, and ledger.py at 518-523. None applies the statement to a mixed composite with H moved and the fermions held fixed. All of them use it for masses, or for gauge-invariant observables, and gauge invariance already implies that all fields transform together. So the trigger in the audit's own what_would_change_the_grade is not met, and NARROWED is not supported.

The audit's scope note (i) is accurate but somewhat over-cautious, since "gauge-invariant" already implies a joint transformation of all fields. It does not change the grade. The tree-level hypothesis is unnamed in the tree but harmless, as the audit says. No measured datum enters the result, so DATA-DEPENDENT cannot be reached. source.located: Classic sources: Sylvester 1852 (law of inertia and the leading-minor criterion) and the discriminant of binary quadratic forms (Lagrange/Gauss). None has an arXiv copy, so all are NAMED-NOT-READ. Read instead through two arXiv restatements. (1) Zhang & Ding, arXiv:2501.00894v1 [math.RA] (2025), p.2, Theorem 1: '(i) A symmetric matrix is PD if and only if all of its leading principal minors are positive. (ii) A symmetric matrix is PSD if and only if all of its principal minors are nonnegative.' The paper covers real matrices only, credits (ii) to Prussing (1986), and warns that the leading-minor test has been misapplied to the PSD case. (2) R. Lopez, arXiv:0810.3351v2 [math.DG]: pp.2-3 define a subspace as spacelike, timelike or lightlike when its induced metric is positive definite, of index 1, or degenerate. Prop 1.3 (p.3): a plane in E^3_1 is timelike iff it contains a timelike vector. p.39: 'W = EG - F^2. The surface is spacelike if W > 0 and it is timelike if W < 0'. The proof of Thm 1.1 (p.5) uses the discriminant of <u+lambda v, u+lambda v> = 0.

audits.published_statement: Zhang-Ding 2501.00894, p.2, Thm 1(i): a real symmetric matrix is positive definite iff all its leading principal minors are positive. For the 2x2 matrix [[A,H],[H,C]] that means A > 0 and AC - H^2 > 0. Lopez 0810.3351, p.3 Prop 1.3 and p.39: in E^3_1 a vector plane is timelike (index 1) iff it contains a timelike vector. Its first fundamental form W = EG - F^2 is spacelike when W > 0, timelike when W < 0, and degenerate/lightlike when W = 0 (p.3, type (3)).
published_hypotheses: Sylvester (read via 2501.00894): the matrix is real and symmetric, and the inequalities are STRICT. The leading-minor test decides only positive definiteness; positive semidefiniteness needs all principal minors (Prussing 1986).
Lopez: the ambient space is E^3_1 (index 1, two spatial dimensions), and the object is a vector plane of dimension exactly 2.
Lopez: the causal character of a subspace is defined by its induced metric: positive definite, index 1, or degenerate.
hypothesis_drift: WIDENED dimension (latticectc.py:40-47, 126-127, 232). The source I read states the result in E^3_1, but the tree uses R^{1,d}: the witness is in R^{1,3} and the census is in R^{1,2}. The law of inertia covers the extension, and I re-derived it here. z3 finds no 2-plane with A<0 and AC-H^2>0 in R^{1,1}, R^{1,2} or R^{1,3}. The scalar z3 checks hold in every dimension. The signed Cauchy-Binet identity was checked symbolically for d = 1 to 4. By hand, for any d: a negative-definite 2-plane would have to meet the t=0 hyperplane, where the form is positive definite. The drift is harmless.

SCOPE of rank (latticectc.py:40, '(c) n >= 2: with Gram entries A, C, H'). The 2x2 Gram test is a statement about rank exactly 2. I built a rational rank-3 example in R^{1,3} in which all three 2-spans are spacelike, yet -3g1+2g2+2g3 has norm -242/9, so it is timelike. The leading minors of the full 3x3 Gram are 106/9, 1675/12 and -46591/36, so Sylvester applied to the full Gram catches it. No computation in the tree applies the 2x2 test at n >= 3 (every check is rank 2: latticectc.py:232-243, 381-393). LEDGER.md:44 (D21) states the rank >= 2 case in terms of 'the span', which is correct when the full Gram is used.

ADDED but not needed: 'exact rational Gram entries'. The rational point m/n exists for real entries too, because the interval between the roots is open and nonempty (checks A3 and A4). Exactness is a property of how the tree verifies the result, not a hypothesis of the theorem.

UNSTATED CONSEQUENCE of that rational hypothesis. If A and H are rational and H^2 = AC, then Q(-H,A) = A(AC-H^2) = 0, so a degenerate span always holds a null lattice vector. Example: g1=(0,1,0), g2=(1,1,1); then g2-g1=(1,0,1) is null, which by (a) gives a closed causal curve that is not timelike. The boundary example at latticectc.py:54-58 correctly needs an irrational s. As a result, 'exactly when the span is spacelike' at LEDGER.md:44 is exact except on the measure-zero set of degenerate spans. This is a discrepancy of phrasing, recorded and not repaired.
A>0 is redundant (latticectc.py:40, 196-197). In R^{1,d}, AC-H^2>0 already forces A>0 (check C1). In the timelike branch, A>0 only rules out the trivial case where g1 is itself causal.
The PSD pitfall named in 2501.00894 p.2 is not incurred. span_kind (latticectc.py:189-198) uses the strict test and puts det = 0 in its own 'degenerate' class.

source.located: arXiv:0802.0658v1 [gr-qc], 5 Feb 2008, B. L. Hu & E. Verdaguer, 'Stochastic Gravity: Theory and Applications' (Feb 2008 update of the 2003 Living Reviews review). Eqs. (3.11)-(3.13) are on p.10 (Sec. 3.2), (3.14)-(3.17) on pp.11-12, (4.11) on p.20 and (5.17) on p.29 (Sec. 5.2.1).

audits.published_statement: From p.10, Sec. 3.2: 'N_abcd[g;x,y) = (1/2) <{t_ab[g;x), t_cd[g;y)}>, (3.11) ... t_ab = T_ab - <T_ab>. (3.12) ... The bi-tensor N_abcd is real and positive semi-definite, as a consequence of T^R_ab being self-adjoint. ... Let us now introduce a Gaussian stochastic tensor field xi_ab[g;x) defined by the following correlators: <xi_ab[g;x)>_s = 0, <xi_ab[g;x) xi_cd[g;y)>_s = N_abcd[g;x,y), (3.13) where <...>_s means statistical average. The symmetry and positive semi-definite property of the noise kernel guarantees that the stochastic field tensor xi_ab ... is well defined. Note that this stochastic tensor captures only partially the quantum nature of the fluctuations of the stress-energy operator since it assumes that cumulants of higher order are zero.' In the paper, xi then sources the Einstein-Langevin equation (3.14) for a linear perturbation h of a background that solves the semiclassical equation (3.7). Its purpose is set by (3.16)-(3.17): the stochastic two-point correlations of h equal the symmetrized quantum two-point correlations, to leading order in 1/N.
published_hypotheses: The spacetime (M, g_ab) is globally hyperbolic and four-dimensional (p.7).
The matter is a real FREE (linear) scalar field of mass m with curvature coupling xi, action (3.1): 'we just assume a scalar field for simplicity'.
N is defined in a general state |psi> with self-adjoint renormalized T^R_ab (Eq. 3.11). The vacuum is a special case; the abstract's 'vacuum expectation value' refers to that case.
N has no UV divergence at separated points for a linear field (p.10). The coincidence limit has meaning only as a distribution (pp.10, 12); Sec. 5.2.1 says divergences occur in that limit.
N is real, symmetric and positive semi-definite, which is what makes the field in (3.13) well defined.
The field is GAUSSIAN: all cumulants above second order are set to zero. This is the stated reason it 'captures only partially the quantum nature'.
The background g_ab solves the semiclassical Einstein equations (3.7), and xi lives on that background independently of h.
The theory works to linear order in the metric perturbation h (Eq. 3.14).
For N fields the correlator is 1/N times one field's noise kernel. The correspondence (3.17) holds to leading order in 1/N.

Scope of use: (3.13) is used only for two-point symmetrized correlations of h ((3.16)-(3.17)) and the Feynman-Vernon identity (4.11). The paper makes no claim about the one-point law or tail probabilities of T_ab.
hypothesis_drift: Not a drift, it matches: noise.py:133-134 says 'N = <{t,t}>/2 is the FULL connected variance'. That is Eq. (3.11) verbatim, and for a real sampler N(f,f) = <t(f)^2> = Var_psi[T(f)] exactly.

A normalisation discrepancy in the literature, recorded and not repaired, with no effect on the tree: the same source's Eq. (5.17) (p.29) writes 8N = <{t,t}>, and Bates 1305.3755 Eq. (4)/(7b) writes N = <{t,t}> with no 1/2. The tree follows (3.11) and in any case uses the variance directly (K_F from formula (V), checked against FFR 1204.3570 Table I).

The reason clause of the caveat is left out at noise.py:169-171: the tree quotes 'captures only partially the quantum nature' verbatim but not 'since it assumes that cumulants of higher order are zero'. This is not a drift in content, because the tree's H6/C1 split (noise.py:22-34, 162-171) states a stronger fact.

An added reading, which the tree discloses: noise.py:46-53 and 344-360 read the one-point law of the smeared xi_00 as the probability of a density outcome, erfc(z/sqrt2)/2. H&V make no one-point or tail claim. The tree labels this 'a different reading of distribution, NOT H6' and calls it a 'surrogate' (noise.py:46-48, 166-171, 293-296).

H&V's background hypothesis (3.7) holds only in the flat model, and the tree leaves this implicit. The Minkowski vacuum satisfies it, so the vacuum-kernel number is inside H&V's hypotheses as a FLAT figure. The corridor does not satisfy it: its demand is not <T^R> of any state, and H2 fails by b/l_G = 61.237 (noise.py:36-44). The sentence at noise.py:46-53 gives the number 'at b = 1 m' without repeating the flat/SURVEY qualifier from noise.py:36-44.

Not a drift: the tree's free minimally coupled scalar (xi = 0, m = 0 in the variance) is inside H&V's action (3.1). It uses a single field rather than large N, and the large-N correspondence (3.17) is not used.
Not a drift: the tree takes only the vacuum noise kernel and refuses non-vacuum kernels (noise.py:51-53, 226-227; EL_SURROGATE_NONVACUUM_COMPUTED = False).

audits.lacked_data: In 2008 the authors did not have the full probability distributions of smeared stress-tensor measurements; FFR published them in 2010 and 2012, and Bates followed in 2013. Having those distributions does not change H&V's conclusion. H&V never claimed the Gaussian source is the quantum law: p.10 says it 'captures only partially the quantum nature ... since it assumes that cumulants of higher order are zero'. The source's stated job, (3.16)-(3.17) and (4.11), needs only the second cumulant, and the smeared kernels are positive (checks B and C1). The later data quantifies the caveat rather than overturning it: skewness is 12 sqrt(2), and the Gaussian puts 45 percent (for phi^2) or 24 percent (for the tree's rho) of its mass below a floor the quantum law never crosses (checks C7 and C8b). The later data does not change the tree's conclusion either. The tree uses the Gaussian tail only as a surrogate labelled 'NOT H6'. On the negative tail the true law is stricter than the surrogate: under H6 the probability at the demand is exactly 0 in the flat model (C1), against exp(-10^141.916) from the surrogate. So restating the demand as a distribution refuses exactly what it refused before, under either reading. The definition has no numerical input that could move. The tree's number depends only on G (unchanged in CODATA 2022), on hbar and c (exact), and on the tree's own K_F and D.

The hypotheses fit the tree's use: it applies (3.13) only to the free minimally coupled scalar in the Minkowski vacuum, which is inside H&V's action (3.1) and solves (3.7). It uses (3.13) only as a surrogate distinct from H6 and refuses non-vacuum kernels. All 22 re-derivation checks pass. exp(-10^141.91579497495206) is reproduced independently to 1e-14, and the CORRECTED entry is confirmed. The smeared noise-kernel variances are exact in sympy. H&V's caveat is confirmed by an exact third cumulant, which also reproduces FFR 1004.0179 Eq. (26). No datum has moved. G is unchanged in CODATA 2022, and the exponent sits 0.084 below 142 and 0.916 above 141, so K_F would have to move by a factor of 0.82 or 8.2 to cross either one. Three named caveats do not lower the grade. First, the one-point tail reading is the tree's own, not H&V's, and the tree says so. Second, H&V's background hypothesis holds only in the flat model, and noise.py:46-53 does not repeat the flat/SURVEY qualifier beside the number. Third, N is normalised differently in (3.11), (5.17) and Bates Eq. (4); no tree figure depends on which is meant.
audits.what_would_change_the_grade: The grade would become NARROWED if the figure exp(-10^141.916) were quoted as a physical probability, or as holding on the curved corridor, without its 'NOT H6' and flat (H2) qualifiers. H&V define (3.13) on a background that solves (3.7) and claim second-order statistics only, and the corridor fails both (3.7) and H2. It would become DATA-DEPENDENT only if the tree's own K_F moved by a factor of 0.82 or 8.2, or if D moved by an equivalent amount. It would become WRONG only with a computed contradiction of (3.11)-(3.13), such as a non-positive smeared noise kernel, and none of the 22 checks found one.

audits.name: Teleportation requires 2 classical bits per qubit; without them B is maximally mixed (Bennett, Brassard, Crepeau, Jozsa, Peres & Wootters, PRL 70, 1895 (1993); the lower bound as restated by Bennett et al. 2001 and proved for exact schemes by Werner 2001)

source.located: Primary: C.H. Bennett, G. Brassard, C. Crepeau, R. Jozsa, A. Peres, W.K. Wootters, 'Teleporting an unknown quantum state via dual classical and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen channels', Phys. Rev. Lett. 70, 1895 (1993). It predates quant-ph and has no arXiv copy, so the paper itself is NAMED-NOT-READ. Restatements READ at alphaXiv: (i) Pirandola, Eisert, Weedbrook, Furusawa, Braunstein, 'Advances in quantum teleportation', arXiv:1505.07831v1 pp.1-2 (the protocol and its hypotheses); (ii) Bennett, DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal, Wootters, 'Remote State Preparation', arXiv:quant-ph/0006044v5 (PRL 87, 077902 (2001)) p.1 (the statement that 2 bits are necessary); (iii) R.F. Werner, 'All teleportation and dense coding schemes', arXiv:quant-ph/0003070v1 (J. Phys. A 34, 7081 (2001)), Thm 1 and its corollary, pp.5-7 (the d^2 lower bound for exact schemes, proved).
source.via: alphaXiv answer_pdf_queries on 1505.07831, quant-ph/0003070 and quant-ph/0006044; the page text they returned was read. Every statement attributed below to Bennett 1993 is quoted from these restatements, which cite it as their ref. [2]/[BB]/[1].

audits.published_statement: Protocol, from Pirandola et al. 2015 restating Bennett et al. 1993 (pp.1-2): Alice and Bob 'share two qubits, A and B, prepared in a pure entangled state. In the ideal case, this is taken to be maximally entangled ... Alice is given another qubit a whose state rho is unknown. She then performs ... Bell detection, which projects her qubits a and A into one of the four Bell states (P_k x I)|Phi> ... Bob's qubit B is simultaneously projected onto P_k^dag rho P_k. In the last (feed-forward) step ... Alice communicates the classical outcome k ... to Bob, who then applies P_k to recover the original input state rho. Note that Alice's input state is assumed to be unknown, otherwise the protocol reduces to remote state preparation.' Also: 'This process requires classical communication and excludes superluminal communication.' NECESSITY, from Bennett et al. 2001 (p.1): 'Two bits of forward classical communication and one ebit of entanglement ... per teleported qubit are both necessary and sufficient, and neither resource can be traded off against the other.' BOUND FOR EXACT SCHEMES, from Werner 2001 (pp.6-7): 'no teleportation ... scheme exists with n < d^2 ... a corollary of Theorem 1', where n is the number of classical signals and d the input dimension. Every tight scheme has a pure maximally entangled resource, unitary corrections and a complete von Neumann measurement.
published_hypotheses: H1: the sender does not know the input state (it is arbitrary, and may be part of a larger entangled system). Pirandola et al. 2015, p.2: 'otherwise the protocol reduces to remote state preparation'.

H2: exact (F = 1) teleportation needs one pure, maximally entangled pair per qubit. A partially entangled pure two-qubit resource teleports perfectly 'if and only if' it is maximally entangled (2506.18577 p.2, citing Li-Li-Guo 2000).
H3: a complete Bell measurement with four outcomes. Incomplete Bell detection makes the protocol post-selected or probabilistic (Pirandola et al. 2015, p.4).

H4: 'Necessary 2 bits' has two meanings. For an exact single-shot scheme with a d x d resource, at least d^2 signals are needed (Werner Thm 1, tight case). As an asymptotic rate, 2 classical bits per qubit are needed however much entanglement is shared beforehand (quant-ph/0006044 p.1).

H5: classical communication runs forward only, over an ordinary channel. The theorem says only that classical communication is required. That the channel is limited to <= c comes from relativity, not from this theorem.
H6: linear quantum mechanics, in which local operations on a shared state cannot signal (the no-communication theorem).
hypothesis_drift: DROPPED (H1, input unknown to the sender) at transit.py:140 'CLASSICAL_BITS_PER_QUBIT = 2', with the selftest label 'classical bits required per qubit' at :335 and transit.py:37-39 and :209-210. The 2-bit requirement is proved only for an input the sender does not know. If the sender knows the state (remote state preparation, RSP), the asymptotic cost is 1 bit per qubit (quant-ph/0006044 p.1). For known equatorial states 1 bit is exactly enough (Pati 1999); rederivation N3 reproduces this with fidelity 1.000000000000000. The tree's 'object in transition' (transit.py:57-60) never says whether the sender knows its state. The count therefore narrows. The refusal built on it does not: RSP still needs at least 1 bit per qubit 'by causality', and without that bit B's averaged state is still I/2 (N3, deviation 5.6e-16).

DROPPED (H4, the derivation) at transit.py:140 and :335. The lower bound is hard-coded, and the selftest compares the constant with itself, which proves nothing. The number is still correct under H1-H3. N1 rederives it from a reference system R: I(R;B_out) <= I(R;B) + log2 k = log2 k, and exact teleportation needs I(R;B_out) = 2, so k >= 4. The standard protocol meets the bound exactly (I(R;BM) = H(M) = 2.000000000000). Werner 2001's corollary proves the same bound. The fault is in the evidence the tree gives for the number, not in the number.

NARROWED IN WORDING (H2), in the entry name 'without them B is maximally mixed' and transit.py:37 'EXACTLY I/2'. B is exactly I/2 only with a maximally entangled resource. With c0|00>+c1|11>, sympy check S2 gives diag(c0^2, c1^2). That is still independent of the input, so 'zero information' holds for every resource. The tree's own protocol uses a Bell pair (transit.py:89), so its instance is correct; only the general reading of the sentence goes too far.

OVERSTATED (interpretation) at transit.py:38-39, :209-210 and paper/CLAIMS.md:4620, 'The state does not exist at the far end until two classical bits arrive'. The theorem says B's state averaged over Alice's unknown outcome carries no information. On each individual outcome, B's qubit is in the state P_k^dag rho P_k (S1 confirms each branch is exactly sigma_m psi). Recorded as a difference of description, not of number.

IMPORTED (H5), correctly flagged by the canonical entry, at transit.py:38-39 and :138-141. The '<= c' comes from relativity. advantage_over_light(D) = arrival_time(D) - D/C_SI with arrival_time(D) = D/C_SI, so it is zero by definition (N4). The four '0.000' rows (transit.py:246-251, selftest :340-341) therefore restate the <= c assumption; they are not a measurement against light. index3.py:1366 rightly says the refusal is proved, but the proof is no-communication plus the <= c assumption, not the printed numbers.
FAITHFUL: b_state_without_bits (transit.py:129-136) computes exactly the quantity the theorem is about. S1 gives exactly I/2 for a symbolic input, so the 1.1e-16 at :37 is float rounding.
FAITHFUL: teleport() (transit.py:113-126) gives four outcomes at p = 1/4 each, and the Pauli corrections restore psi exactly, confirmed symbolically in S1.

rederivation.outcome: ALL CHECKS PASS (exit 0). S1 (sympy, exact, symbolic input): each outcome has p = 1/4, the Pauli corrections restore psi exactly, and rho_B with the bits withheld is exactly I/2, whatever the input. S2 (sympy): with resource cos t|00>+sin t|11>, rho_B without bits is diag(cos^2 t, sin^2 t). It carries no information about the input but is not I/2. N1 (lower bound via a reference system R): I(R;B) = 8.9e-16 before any message. Exact teleportation needs I(R;B_out) = 2 on every branch. Since I(R;B_out) <= I(R;BM) <= I(R;B) + log2 k for a classical message with k values, k >= 4. The standard protocol meets this exactly (I(R;BM) = H(M) = 2.000000000000). This inequality chain is a proof, not a numerical fit. N2: coarse-grained Bell schemes with k = 3 and k = 2 reach only 1.5 and 1.0 bits. 200 random protocols for each k = 2, 3, 4 stay within the bound; this is a sanity check only, since random search does not reach the extreme cases. An initialisation bug in this check was found and fixed before the final run. N3: RSP of known equatorial states with 1 bit gives minimum fidelity 1.000000000000000 over 50 states, and without the bit B is I/2 (deviation 5.6e-16). N4: transit.py's no-bits deviation is float rounding (at most 3.33e-16 over 1000 inputs), and advantage_over_light is D/c - D/c = 0 by definition.

later_literature.ref: R.F. Werner, 'All teleportation and dense coding schemes', arXiv:quant-ph/0003070 (J. Phys. A 34, 7081 (2001))
later_literature.what: Proves that no exact teleportation scheme for a d-level system with a d x d resource uses fewer than d^2 classical signals, and that every tight scheme is the standard one: maximally entangled resource, unitary corrections, complete von Neumann measurement. For d = 2 that is 4 signals, i.e. 2 bits. This is the derivation the tree hard-codes.

later_literature.ref: C.H. Bennett et al., 'Remote State Preparation', arXiv:quant-ph/0006044 (PRL 87, 077902 (2001))
later_literature.what: States that teleportation needs 2 classical bits and 1 ebit per qubit and that neither can be traded for the other. For a known state, the asymptotic cost is 1 bit per qubit, with 1 bit as the floor by causality. Lo's 2 log d conjecture is proved only for oblivious, exactly faithful protocols with unitary corrections. This narrows the tree's '2' to unknown inputs and leaves the no-faster-than-light conclusion intact.

later_literature.ref: S. Pirandola et al., 'Advances in quantum teleportation', arXiv:1505.07831 (2015)
later_literature.what: Restates the protocol and its hypotheses and says it 'excludes superluminal communication'. d-level schemes use d^2 signals. In port-based teleportation, fidelity reaches 1 only as the number of ports grows. Reviews experiments with real-time feed-forward.

later_literature.what: Perfect qubit teleportation through partially entangled two-qutrit channels. The classical message needs at least 2 bits (Shannon entropy), reaching 2 only when the channel reduces to a Bell pair. Consistent with 2 bits as the floor.

later_literature.what: One classical bit cannot perfectly teleport even the l1-coherence of an arbitrary unknown qubit. It works only for partially known states (equatorial or polar circles).

later_literature.what: Remote state preparation for special ensembles, and Lo's conjecture. Used here only as restated in quant-ph/0006044; the equatorial protocol is reproduced in N3.

audits.lacked_data: Testing M's hypothesis that earlier physicists lacked data: Bennett et al. 1993 is a theorem of finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, and its conclusion depends on no measured quantity. The tree's only numbers are a float-rounding residual, an integer, and c, which is exact by definition. Three things came after 1993. (a) The optimality proof for exact schemes (Werner 2001) confirms 2 bits for an unknown input. (b) Remote state preparation (Pati 1999, Lo 1999, Bennett et al. 2001) lowers the cost to 1 bit per qubit when the sender knows the state. That is a real narrowing, discovered later. (c) Experiments with real-time feed-forward (reviewed in 1505.07831) report no arrival without the classical message. Weighing both directions: later knowledge changes the count for known inputs from 2 to 1, and changes nothing in the tree's refusal. The refusal needs only two things. First, no-signalling: B's averaged state does not depend on the input until the message arrives, which is rederived exactly here for every resource (S1, S2) and for RSP (N3). Second, the classical channel travelling at no more than c (H5, audited under the c entry). Changing the conclusion would take a violation of no-signalling in linear quantum mechanics. Nothing in the literature read here shows one, and none is presumed.
audits.grade_evidence: The theorem holds as stated, and the tree's instance reproduces exactly. S1 gives rho_B = I/2 identically for a symbolic input, so the tree's 1.1e-16 is rounding. There are four outcomes at p = 1/4 and fidelity 1 after correction. The 2 bits are rederived as a lower bound that the standard protocol meets exactly (N1), matching Werner 2001's n >= d^2. The narrowing has two parts. (1) The tree says '2 classical bits required per qubit' (transit.py:140, :335) without the hypothesis that the sender does not know the input. For known states, remote state preparation needs 1 bit per qubit asymptotically and exactly 1 for equatorial states (N3). (2) 'Exactly I/2' needs a maximally entangled resource (S2), although 'zero information' holds for any resource. Neither narrowing reaches the conclusion the tree rests on this result (advantage 0, and the consumers D23, R11, Rec): every protocol, RSP included, still needs at least 1 classical bit, and until it arrives B's state does not depend on the input. Three further discrepancies are recorded but not graded: the selftest's 2-bit check compares the constant with itself; the advantage over light is zero by definition; and 'the state does not exist at the far end' says more than the theorem does. The grade is not WRONG, because nothing refutes the source, and not DATA-DEPENDENT, because no measured quantity enters it.
audits.what_would_change_the_grade: To STANDS: transit.py:140/:335 names H1 ('for an input the sender does not know; a known state needs only 1 bit per qubit via RSP, still at least 1 by causality') and names the maximally-entangled condition for 'exactly I/2'. Showing that the tree's use case requires an unknown input would also do it. To WRONG: an exact scheme that teleports arbitrary unknown qubits with fewer than 4 classical signals, or a protocol in which B's state before the message depends on the input. To DATA-DEPENDENT: an experiment showing such input dependence. None is known in the literature read here. Reading PRL 70, 1895 itself would raise the read status but is not expected to change the grade.

It matches transit.py's teleport() and b_state_without_bits() at transit.py:113-136, with the same Bell ordering and the same CORRECTIONS [I, X, Z, ZX]. S2 correctly separates "exactly I/2", which needs a maximally entangled resource, from "zero information", which holds for any resource.

The general lower bound in N1 (I(R;B_out) <= I(R;BM) = I(R;B) + I(R;M|B) <= 0 + H(M|B) <= log2 k) is printed as text, not machine-checked. I checked each step: data processing on Bob's side, the chain rule, H(M|RB) >= 0 for a classical M, and I(R;B) = 0 by no-signalling. The argument is valid, and it does not assume a d x d resource, so it is more general than Werner's tight-scheme setting. The code itself only confirms that the standard protocol meets the bound exactly. N2's random search is weak: the closest a random protocol gets is -0.39 bits below the bound. The audit labels N2 a sanity check, and the k=2 coarse-grained scheme reaches log2 k exactly, so the entropy calculation does get tested at the bound.

N3 is a single example (equatorial states with a Z/I correction that does not depend on the state). It shows that 1 bit can be enough. The asymptotic 1 bit per qubit for remote state preparation (RSP) is taken from quant-ph/0006044, not rederived.

**Vacuity guards** (vacuity_s.py and vacuity.py, all behave as expected):
- V1: swapping the X and Z corrections is detected as failing to restore psi (symbolic).
- V1b: a 1-bit correction rule {I,X,I,X} fails for an unknown psi, so a negated H1 shows up in the exact test.
- V2: replacing the classical message with a 2-dimensional quantum one gives I(R;Q) = 2 > log2 2. The classical-message hypothesis carries weight in N1.
- V3: the 1-bit equatorial RSP scheme drops to an average fidelity of 0.5197 off the equator, so N3 is specific and does not pass trivially.
- V4: the input-independence test in S2 does detect a matrix that depends on psi.
- V5: I(R;B) = 0 (at most 8.9e-16) for random 3x3 resources after random unitaries on Alice's side, so N1's premise holds beyond the Bell-pair case.
- V6: the entropy calculator reports I(R;B) = 2 when B starts correlated with R.

The checks are not vacuous, and they encode the theorem rather than a weaker version of it.

**Grade.** The tree's numbers reproduce exactly. The 2-bit constant at transit.py:140 is still compared only with itself at :335. That is confirmed by reading the source, and it is a fault in the evidence, not in the value. Two narrowings survive:
1. The H1 condition (sender does not know the input) is unstated. With V1b and N3/V3, this is a real difference for known states.
2. "Exactly I/2" holds only for a maximally entangled resource (S2).

Neither narrowing reaches the refusal. Every scheme keeps B independent of the input until the message arrives (S1, S2, N3, V5). One caveat could move the grade to STANDS: a physical "object in transition" that is entangled with its surroundings arguably requires an input the sender does not know. The audit already names this route, and it is a matter of interpretation, not something computed here. I found nothing that supports WRONG or DATA-DEPENDENT.

verifiers.lens: THE DATA CLAIM: each data_at_publication row and the lacked_data answer checked at source (quant-ph/0006044, quant-ph/0003070 and 1505.07831 read again through alphaXiv) and against transit.py, loaded by path
verifiers.reason:
The grade NARROWED survives this lens. No row's moves_conclusion is reversed, but five data claims need correcting.

ROW 1 (deviation of rho_B from I/2): value_then is right. transit.py prints 1.1e-16 (report line 99, docstring :37), and the selftest check is dev < 1e-14 over 3 trials. That check sits at :334, not :332. value_now 'exactly 0' holds: S1 reruns PASS, exit 0. Discrepancy: the claim 'at most 3.33e-16 over 1000 inputs' is attributed to transit.py, but N4 never loads transit.py. It recomputes the quantity with its own numpy code. Loaded by path, transit.py's own b_state_without_bits gives a maximum deviation of 4.996e-16 over 1000 random_unitary inputs (seed 12345). Still rounding, so moves_conclusion 'no' follows. The number should not be quoted as transit.py's.

ROW 2 (bits per qubit): value_then '2, hard-coded at :140' is correct, and the selftest at :335 checks the constant against itself. Werner's corollary was read at source (pp.6-7). It is proved by padding signals and applying Theorem 1, and Theorem 1 assumes the resource omega lives on H x H. So it covers d x d resources only. N1's reference-system argument is what covers a resource of any size; row 2 credits both without saying this. More serious: the RSP part of value_now and moves_conclusion leaves out conditions that quant-ph/0006044 states. (a) The 1-bit asymptotic cost holds 'in the presence of a large amount of prior entanglement'. That is about 2^n ebits per state, or e' about 3.79 ebits per qubit with back communication (p.2). (b) It is an expected cost of a block protocol. For finite n: 'We know of no exactly faithful RSP protocol for finite n that always uses less classical communication than would be required by teleportation. In this sense Lo's conjecture still stands' (p.2). Lo's 2 log d bound is proved there for oblivious, exactly faithful protocols with unitary corrections (pp.2-3). (c) Fig. 1 puts teleportation at (e=1, b=2) and shows no protocol at 1 ebit with b < 2 for generic states. transit.py's resource is one Bell pair per transit (one pair, one transit). Under that budget the literature read here does not lower the count for a generic known qubit below 2. So the unqualified 'It moves the count for known states from 2 to 1' overstates the narrowing against the tree. The narrowing itself is real. The equatorial one-bit protocol (Pati, quoted exactly at source on p.1) uses one singlet and one bit, and N3 reproduces it with F = 1.000000000000000. That alone carries NARROWED. 'Floor 1 bit by causality' is read correctly: p.2 says 'necessary [3] by causality', and Fig. 1 says b < 1 is inaccessible.

ROW 3 (c): C_SI = 2.99792458e8 equals exactly 299792458.0 (checked). It sits at transit.py:142, not :138; arrival_time is at :145 and advantage_over_light at :146. advantage_over_light returns [0, 0, 0, 0], zero by definition, as the audit says. moves_conclusion 'no' follows.

LACKED_DATA: M's hypothesis is answered with evidence. The theorem's conclusion depends on no measured quantity: the only numbers are a rounding residual, an integer, and an SI-exact c. The later work found is a real narrowing (RSP) and an optimality proof (Werner); both were read. One claim is unsupported at source: '(c) Experiments with real-time feed-forward (reviewed in 1505.07831) report no arrival without the classical message.' 1505.07831 pp.4 and 8 describe real-time feed-forward experiments and their fidelities: 89% at 16 km, 69% for transmon qubits, 86% for NV centres. None of them is reported as testing, or finding, that B has no information without the message. That clause must be removed or marked NOT-READ-AT-SOURCE. It leans in the tree's favour, and the refusal needs it from no source, since no-signalling is a theorem here (S1, S2, N3).

Net: the conclusion and the grade NARROWED stand. Five corrections are needed, all recorded and none repaired: (1) attribute N4's 3.33e-16 to its own reimplementation, not to transit.py; transit.py itself gives 4.996e-16 at seed 12345. (2) Name RSP's hypotheses in row 2: large prior entanglement (about 3.79 ebits per qubit with back communication), asymptotic expected cost, and Lo's conjecture still standing for exact finite-n protocols. Under the tree's one-ebit budget only special ensembles such as equatorial states drop to 1 bit. (3) Werner's corollary covers d x d resources only. (4) Remove the experimental 'no arrival' attribution from lacked_data(c). (5) Fix the line references: C_SI at :142, selftest at :334.

audits.name: Anglada et al. 2017: ALMA 1.3 mm detection of a 1-4 au dust belt around Proxima Cen, ~0.01 M_earth total by -3.5 size-law extrapolation to 50 km; 0.4 au warm dust and ~30 au belt marginal; 1.3 mm traces um-cm grains

source.located: G. Anglada et al., 'ALMA Discovery of Dust Belts Around Proxima Centauri', arXiv:1711.00578v1 [astro-ph.EP], 2 Nov 2017 (ApJL 850 L6). Secs 1, 2, 3.1-3.4, abstract.
source.via: alphaXiv get_paper_content(fullText=true): whole v1 read incl. references. The journal version (ApJL 850 L6) was NOT read, so a v1 discrepancy recorded here must not be quoted against the journal version until it is read. Later work READ at source: MacGregor et al. 2018 arXiv:1802.08257 (whole paper); Faria et al. 2022 arXiv:2202.05188 (Table 1, Table C.1, sec 6); Burton et al. 2025 arXiv:2503.21890 (abstract, secs 1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 3.3, 5).

audits.published_statement: Abstract: 'a belt of dust orbiting around it at distances ranging between 1 and 4 au, approximately ... about 40 K ... The estimated total mass, including dust and bodies up to 50 km in size, is of the order of 0.01 Earth masses ... Our data also show a hint of warmer dust closer to the star. We also find signs of two additional features ... which still require further observations to be confirmed: an outer extremely cold (about 10 K) belt at about 30 au ... and a compact 1.3 mm source at ~1.2 arcsec'. Sec 3.2: the ACA source measures 340+/-60 uJy against a 74+/-4 uJy photosphere, with '~200 uJy of dust emission spread over a belt ... ~1.3-4 au'. The dust mass is (m_dust/M_E) = 0.5 (S/Jy)(T/K)^-1 (d/pc)^2 (nu/230 GHz)^-2 with kappa = 2 cm^2/g, and T_d = 278 L^0.25 r^-0.5, giving T_d ~ 40 K and m_d ~ 4e-6 M_E. 'The 1.3 mm continuum emission traces dust grains with um to cm sizes'. The size law has index -3.5 (Tanaka 1996), and 'if the primordial size distribution connects smoothly with the collisional cascade ... m_tot ~ m_dust (D_max/D_dust)^0.5 ... D_dust ~ 1 cm ... m_tot ~ 2200 m_dust (D_max/50 km)^0.5 ... m_tot ~ 1e-2 M_E'. Warm component: 'it might be possible' that ~30 uJy of dust sits at ~0.4 au, with T_d ~ 90 K, m_dust ~5.5e-7 and m_tot ~1e-3 M_E. Sec 3.3: 30 au belt, 1.7 mJy, 10 K, m_dust 1.4e-4 and m_tot 0.33 M_E, 'marginal'. Sec 1: Proxima b m_p sin i = 1.3 M_E at 0.05 au, cited from Anglada-Escude 2016.
published_hypotheses: H1: the ACA flux above the photosphere (~270 uJy) is steady thermal dust emission. The stellar term is the Ribas 2017 photospheric model (74 uJy) plus negligible non-thermal emission; all epochs are combined and no time-variability analysis is reported.
H2: the ~200 uJy the 12-m array misses is spread over more than ~7 beams, so it sits at radii ~1-3 arcsec (~1.3-4 au).
H3: the dust opacity is kappa_nu = 2 cm^2/g at 230 GHz (Beckwith 2000), the emission is optically thin, and the Rayleigh-Jeans form holds (implicit).
H4: T_d = 278 (L/Lsun)^0.25 (r/au)^-0.5 (Wyatt 2008), with L = 0.0015 Lsun (Ribas 2017) and d = 1.3 pc (van Leeuwen 2007).
H5: 1.3 mm continuum traces um-cm grains; D_dust ~ 1 cm.
H6: the collisional-cascade equilibrium size distribution has index -3.5 (Tanaka 1996).
H7: the primordial size distribution connects smoothly with the cascade (Wyatt & Dent 2002).
H8: the extrapolation runs to D_max ~ 50 km, with m_tot scaling as (D_max/50 km)^0.5.

H9: the authors state that their 'data are insufficient for a proper modeling', so the masses are rough estimates. The 0.4 au component is a 'hint'; the 30 au belt and the 1.2 arcsec source are 'marginal'.
H10: Proxima b m_p sin i = 1.3 M_E at 0.05 au is imported from Anglada-Escude 2016, not measured in this paper.
hypothesis_drift: DROPPED (formation.py:283-285, 443): the tree names only the -3.5 size law and the 50 km cap. It drops H3 (kappa = 2 cm^2/g, optically thin, Rayleigh-Jeans), H4 (the T_d law, L and d), H5's D_dust ~ 1 cm and H7 (the smooth connection). The ~0.01 M_E depends on all of these, not on the size law alone. The tree only reports the number and then withdraws it, so this is not an over-claim.

DROPPED (formation.py:283-287): H1, that the ACA excess is steady dust emission, is not named at the Anglada line. The tree does record its failure right after, at formation.py:286-290 and 458 (SURVEY_BELT_1_4AU_WITHDRAWN_BY_SOURCE = True, citing MacGregor 2018 sec 4.2).

SITE DISCREPANCY (formation.py:284-285, 443-444): the tree writes 'Warm dust at ~0.4 au and a ~30 au belt are both marginal (abstract, 3.3)'. The 0.4 au component is in sec 3.2, not 3.3. The abstract gives no radius, only 'a hint of warmer dust closer to the star'. The paper uses 'marginal' only for the 30 au belt and the 1.2 arcsec source; for the warm dust it says 'hint' and 'might be possible'. MacGregor 2018 sec 4.2 paraphrases both as 'marginal detections'. This is a citation and wording discrepancy; there is no change of substance.
CONSISTENT (formation.py:283): '1-4 au' is the abstract's 'between 1 and 4 au, approximately'; sec 3.2 derives ~1.3-4 au.

RETAINED (formation.py:298-299, 463): the quote 'traces dust grains with um to cm sizes' is verbatim from sec 3.2. SURVEY_CONSTRAINS_BODIES = False agrees with the source, whose body masses are extrapolated, not measured.

SECOND-HAND DATUM (formation.py:292-295, 452-453): Proxima b's 1.3 M_E at 0.05 au is correctly read from Anglada sec 1, which imports it from Anglada-Escude 2016. The value has since moved to 1.07 +/- 0.06 M_E at 0.04856 au (Faria 2022 Table C.1). This does not change the tree's use.

audits.lacked_data: M's hypothesis is SUPPORTED for this result, with a qualification. Anglada et al. had the relevant data: all 13 ACA sessions at integration level. They combined all epochs and did not analyse them over time. They also lacked the knowledge that M dwarfs flare strongly at millimetre wavelengths. MacGregor 2018 reports the first mm flare from Proxima and notes that M-dwarf mm flares were 'not previously well-studied'; Burton 2025 finds 463 in ~50 h. Having this datum changes the conclusion for the 1-4 au belt and its ~0.01 M_E: there is no quiescent excess, and a flare-only reading reproduces the combined ACA flux (computed here: 261-312 uJy against 334 +/- 48). It plausibly changes the 0.4 au component, since MacGregor's coronal reading is conditional. It does not change the 30 au belt, which was marginal before and remains marginal. Evidence the other way: 'no need to posit' is not a demonstrated absence. A fainter belt below the quiescent ACA limit (rms 68 uJy/beam) is not excluded, and nothing read here gives a belt-mass upper limit. The extrapolation itself (H3-H8) is not refuted by any datum read. It re-derives, apart from one unused v1 discrepancy, and its inputs d and L moved by less than 2%. The failure is in the observational premise H1, not in the size-law mathematics. The tree already marks the belt WITHDRAWN (formation.py:458) and does not rest D25 on it, so D25 stays OPEN/UNDETERMINED. The one stale datum the tree carries from this paper is Proxima b's 1.3 M_E, now 1.07 M_E, which does not move its threshold comparison.
audits.grade_evidence: The published conclusion, a 1-4 au belt of ~0.01 M_E including bodies up to 50 km, moves with a datum that has moved. Re-analysis of the same ACA data shows the excess it rests on (H1) is a ~1 min flare with no quiescent excess (MacGregor 2018 sec 3.2, 4.2, READ); Burton 2025 (READ) confirms that such flares are common. The 0.4 au component is contested and the 30 au belt remains marginal. The extrapolation arithmetic re-derives (rederive A-C, E), apart from one v1 discrepancy in the warm-dust mass (2.8e-7 recomputed against 5.5e-7 printed), which the tree does not use. The grade is not WRONG because nothing read shows the belt absent. It is not STANDS because a moved datum moves the conclusion. NARROWED is not the primary grade because the tree uses the result as reported-then-withdrawn (formation.py:286-290, 458) and rests nothing on the 0.01 M_E. It does drop H1, H3, H4, H5 and H7 from its one-line statement (formation.py:283-285) and mis-sites the 0.4 au component, citing 'abstract, 3.3' where the source is sec 3.2 and calls it a 'hint'.
audits.what_would_change_the_grade: To WRONG: a deep quiescent ALMA, far-IR or JWST limit, read at source, below the ~200 uJy assigned to 1-4 au. None was found. To STANDS for the belt: a confirmed steady mm excess at 1-4 au in data with the flares removed, for example the 2019 campaign's 34 h of ACA data or the 2021 12-m data. For the 30 au belt: an independent detection, or identification of the peaks as background sources. Reading the ApJL 850 L6 journal version would settle whether the warm-dust mass discrepancy is in the record. On the tree side, correcting formation.py:284-285's citation and naming H1, H3 and H4 would bring the statement exactly to source. Updating PROXIMA_B_MSINI_EARTH to 1.07 would change no verdict.

MacGregor: 334+/-48 uJy; no source above 3 sigma in the first 12 sessions at rms 68; final session 1.17+/-0.10 mJy; 100+/-4 mJy flare; 'the entirety of the 1.3 mm emission detected by the ACA results from the short duration stellar flare ... no need to posit the cold belt'; the 0.4 au dust removed only 'if' the 12-m excess is coronal; 13 +10/-8 background sources. Burton: 463 flares in ~50 h; 119+/-7 mJy. Faria: 1.07+/-0.06 M_E at 0.04856 au (TM), 1.15 (CCF); 1.3012 pc; 0.0016 Lsun.

I also checked the numbers independently (verify/refute/1711.00578_check.py). Warm dust from the printed inputs: 30 uJy at 90 K gives 2.82e-7 M_E; even 32 uJy (106-74) gives 3.0e-7; using the paper's own parallax for d changes nothing. Reaching 5.5e-7 needs 58.6 uJy. So the v1 discrepancy is real, and the audit correctly treats it as a discrepancy, not a refutation. Belt: 4.23e-6 x 2236 = 9.45e-3. Inverse-variance combination of the two sub-images: 261/283/312 uJy for first-12 fluxes of 74/101/136, which reproduces the audit's F.

On WRONG: under the docket rubric, WRONG needs a counterexample or computed contradiction SHOWN here. The best I can compute is that a steady ~340 uJy source would be a 5 sigma peak in the first-12 image (rms 68), but only a ~2 sigma peak is seen. That is ~3 sigma tension (~2.5 sigma in the audit's three-component version), and it is approximate. It is not decisive, and it is not a demonstrated absence. MacGregor's refutation of Anglada's attribution ('70-80% ... does not arise from the star') is READ, not computed here. Grading it WRONG would over-represent the result in M's favour.

On STANDS: the sole dust-flux input H1 is contested by a re-analysis of the same data, so STANDS is excluded. NARROWED also formally applies (the tree drops H1, H3, H4, H5 and H7), but the rubric's 'conclusion moves with a datum that has moved or is contested' is the stronger and primary description. The audit says this.

Minor corrections that do not move the grade:
(1) Burton's 119 vs MacGregor's 100 mJy is not cleanly a 'discrepancy between reanalyses'. Burton sec 4.2 says it re-measures 'the same event at higher temporal resolution using 1 s integration times' against MacGregor's 2 s fits. A higher peak at finer sampling is expected, so record it as a resolution difference.
(2) Burton's effect is labelled 'confirms', but Burton never addresses the belts. It confirms only that mm flaring is common; 'supports the flare reading indirectly' is closer.
(3) The drift row says the paper uses 'marginal' only for the 30 au belt and the 1.2 arcsec source. Anglada's Fig. 4 caption reads 'Question marks indicate marginally detected features', and MacGregor sec 4.2 reads Anglada as calling the warm dust and the outer belt 'marginal detections'. The figure text is font-garbled in the extraction, so whether the 0.4 au component carries a '?' is OPEN here. The tree's 'marginal' wording may have source support. The mis-citation 'abstract, 3.3' stands either way: the component is in sec 3.2, and the abstract says only 'hint'.
(4) The lacked_data verdict 'SUPPORTED' leans slightly toward M. By the audit's own account the authors held the session-level data, and Proxima was long known as a flare star (MacGregor sec 1). What they lacked was an analysis step plus the then-unstudied M-dwarf mm-flare behaviour, not data. 'Partly supported' would be more even.

The grade survives. One computed claim that supports it does not: check F, the "flare-only reading reproduces the combined ACA flux", fails the vacuity guard and must be demoted from evidence to an OPEN note.

What reproduces. The copy at verify/rederive/1711.00578.py exits 0 with the same output the audit reports. I re-read the inputs at source: Anglada v1 sec 3.2-3.3 and MacGregor 2018 sec 3.2 and 4.2, through alphaXiv. All of them match the paper: 340+/-60, 74, ~270, ~200 uJy; the 0.5 formula; kappa = 2; the T_d law; D_dust ~ 1 cm; 2200; 50 km; warm ~30 uJy at 90 K printing 5.5e-7; 1.7 mJy at 10 K giving 1.4e-4 and 0.33; and 334+/-48, rms 47/68/150, 1.17+/-0.10 mJy.

Checks A-E encode the published statement itself, not a toy version of it, and they discriminate. With the hypotheses negated:
- kappa = 1 gives a prefactor of 0.98 and FAILS.
- q = -3.4 or -3.6 gives m_tot = 4.4e-2 or 2.0e-3 and FAILS.
- D_dust = 1 mm or 10 cm gives 3.0e-2 or 3.0e-3 and FAILS.
- m_tot's 0.5x-2x window is loose but not vacuous.

The warm-dust discrepancy is real against the printed v1 inputs. 30 uJy at 90 K gives 2.82e-7, and 32 uJy at 86.5 K gives 3.13e-7, against 5.5e-7 printed. Halving T would reproduce 5.5e-7, but that is speculation, not a finding. It stays a v1 discrepancy, unused by the tree, and the journal version is not read.

Defect, in check F. It weights the two sub-images by inverse variance of rms 68 and 150, and that gives a combined rms of 62. MacGregor prints 47 for the 13-session image, so the three printed rms values are not mutually consistent, and the weight of the last session is not determined by what was read. I computed the same test under weightings that are equally defensible:
- Last-session weight from the combined rms (47/150)^2 = 0.098: flare-only gives 182-238 uJy, 2.0-3.2 sigma below 334. Anglada's steady model plus the flare gives 389, only -1.1 sigma.
- Equal sessions, weight 1/13: flare-only gives 158-216, 2.5-3.7 sigma below. Steady plus flare gives 371, -0.8 sigma.

So F's PASS, and its preference for the flare reading, inverts with the weighting choice. Worse, the negated hypothesis "steady 334 uJy in every session" matches the combined flux exactly. Matching the combined flux therefore cannot tell the two readings apart.

The audit's lacked_data and data_at_publication text cite "computed here: 261-312 uJy against 334 +/- 48" as support. That claim must be withdrawn or marked weighting-dependent and OPEN.

What actually carries the moved datum is READ, not computed. MacGregor sec 3.2: no source above 3 sigma in the first 12 sessions at rms 68, while Anglada's model predicts ~304 uJy, about 4.5 sigma, which would have been seen. MacGregor sec 4.2: "the entirety of the 1.3 mm emission detected by the ACA results from the short duration stellar flare". Burton 2025 adds that mm flares are common. The first-12 tension note, (304-136)/68 ~ 2.5 sigma, rests on those READ numbers and stands as approximate.

That READ evidence is enough for DATA-DEPENDENT. H1 has moved and the conclusion moves with it. Nothing read shows the belt absent, so the grade is not WRONG. The size-law arithmetic re-derives, so the failure is in the premise, not the mathematics.

Required corrections to the audit:
- Demote F from PASS to NOTE/OPEN, and state that MacGregor's printed rms values are internally inconsistent: inverse-variance gives 62 against 47 printed. This is a discrepancy in the later paper, recorded, not a refutation of it.
- Remove "computed here" as support for the flare reading.
- Keep the grade.

verifiers.reason:
Checked at source. The data rows that carry the grade hold up:
- **ACA flux.** Anglada gives 340+/-60 uJy against a 74+/-4 photosphere, ~270 excess, ~200 assigned to 1.3-4 au, and says all epochs were combined. MacGregor gives 334+/-48 combined. Its first-12 image has no source above 3 sigma at rms 68, with only a ~2 sigma central peak. The final session is 1.17+/-0.10 mJy, the flare peaks at 100+/-4 mJy over ~1 min, and sec 4.2 says "no need to posit the cold belt at 1-4 AU".
- **12-m flux.** Anglada gives 106+/-12; MacGregor gives 101+/-9, point-like, with any elongation at ~2 sigma and varying. The coronal reading is "plausibly" and explicitly conditional ("If ... then").
- **30 au belt.** 13 (+10/-8) background sources above 150 uJy are expected in the primary beam, and the short spacings are missing.
- **Proxima b.** Faria Table C.1 gives 1.07+/-0.06 M_E at 0.04856 au (TM) and 1.15 (CCF). I recomputed log10(1.07/1.3) = -0.0846.
- **d and L together.** Recomputed factor 0.9858.
- **Burton.** 463 flares in ~50 h; the 2017-03-24 flare is 119+/-7 mJy.

So each moves_conclusion entry follows from what was read. The belt's ~0.01 M_E falls with H1, the 0.4 au component is contested but not refuted, and the 30 au belt stays marginal. None of the corrections below moves the grade.

Corrections, all minor:

(1) **L is not a "moved" datum.** Faria's 0.0016+/-0.0006 is Boyajian 2012, which is older than Anglada's Ribas 2017 value of 0.0015. Its error bar contains 0.0015. It is an alternative literature value, not a value_now. The row's "No" stands.

(2) **The Burton 119 vs MacGregor 100 mJy difference is not unexplained.** Burton sec 3.1 attributes it to its 1 s cadence resolving a peak that MacGregor's lower time resolution did not. It should be recorded as explained.

(3) **The audit omits that Burton Table 2 lists >=8 sigma flares on 1 Feb 2017 (50 and 58 mJy) and 19 Mar 2017 (39 mJy).** Both dates fall inside MacGregor's "first 12" ACA sessions. So "no source above 3 sigma" depends on binning: MacGregor imaged sessions whole and in 30 s bins. This strengthens the flare reading. It does not change the numbers: a 58 mJy, ~5 s flare adds ~4 uJy to a 19 h average.

(4) **The quiescent-tension figure is understated, which is the conservative direction.** Anglada's own quiescent budget in the ACA beam is star 74 + compact ~70 (warm 30 + secondary 38) + belt 200, about 344 uJy, not 304. That gives ~3.1 sigma against the ~2 sigma peak, and an expected S/N of ~5 in the first-12 image.

(5) **"Nothing read here gives a belt-mass upper limit" is too strong.** MacGregor's first-12 rms gives an approximate 3 sigma limit of belt <~103-130 uJy, i.e. m_tot <~5-6e-3 M_E under Anglada's own H3-H8. This is approximate and should be labelled so.

(6) **The lacked_data headline "SUPPORTED" leans toward M.** The datum that undid the belt was in Anglada's own data: all 13 sessions at integration level. What was missing was a time-domain analysis, and the prior that M-dwarf mm flares reach ~100 mJy. MacGregor calls these "not previously well-studied", and Burton says the first Proxima mm flare was found "unexpectedly" in this very dataset. Proxima was long known as a flare star (MacGregor cites Thackeray 1950), and Anglada only extrapolated steady non-thermal emission (Slee 2003, ~1 uJy). The audit states this qualification, but the honest label is PARTLY: the data were held, and the analysis and prior knowledge were lacking. M's rules require avoiding over-representation in both directions.

The grade itself is defensible. DATA-DEPENDENT fits because the conclusion falls with H1, which re-analysis shows false. It is not WRONG because no source read shows the belt absent, only that its detection is unsupported at ~3 sigma. It is not STANDS. audits.lacked_data: In 1975 ICRP 23 lacked in vivo whole-body data for women and for non-Western populations: it carries no Reference Woman elemental data, and in vivo Reference Woman estimates only came in 1990. It also predates the anatomical review that became ICRP 89 (2002) and the ICRP 110 (2009) tissue set. The source itself is not shown wrong. Nothing here contradicts 780 g of P for the defined 1975 male, and its table could not be read. verifiers.reason:
Each data row checks out against what can be read here. Nothing found overturns the audit. The corrections are small, and two of them strengthen the audit rather than weaken it.

ROW BY ROW
(1) Body mass. I re-read Wikipedia 'Standard person' through alphaXiv; a direct curl gets a 403. It quotes ICRP 23 p.335 verbatim (20-30 y, 70 kg, 170 cm, Caucasian). It says 'ICRP-23 ... does not contain elemental data for a "Reference Woman"', and it says the revised Reference Man's 'weight increased by 3 kg'. The page puts that revision under the 1984 decision. It does not name ICRP 89, so tying the 3 kg to P89 is an inference from icrp.org's 'supplemented and amended by P89'. It is plausible, but it was not read as such. moves_conclusion='No' for the per-kg factors is correct, because the factors are ratios of mass fractions.
(2) Phosphorus. value_then is right: 780/70085.9 = 1.1129 %, reproduced. For value_now I re-read Kanematsu arXiv:1508.00226 Table I at source. The m% column and the w_P, w_N and w_C values are exactly as the script encodes them. m is the mass fraction 'per person (50% male/50% female)' over ICRP 110's 53 standard tissues. This reproduces P 0.813 %, N 2.40 %, C 31.6 % and Ca 1.53 %. One caveat, which the audit states: Eq. 1 mass-weights the elemental densities ρw, so each regional w is density-and-mass weighted. The whole body is therefore approximate, but the density spread within a region is small. The restatement's fraction column reads '5-7×10^-3' (wiki line 319), and the same page's infobox gives P 0.6 % by mass (line 193), which is 421 g, also below the 715.7 g flip. The infobox is a second on-page source the audit did not cite. moves_conclusion=YES follows: Li 1752 > P 1395 at the photosphere, and C 9.02 > P 7.81 > N 7.53 at CI, both reproduced in rederive/*.out.
(3) Lithium. The page reads mass 0.000007 kg and fraction 31×10^-9, which gives 2.17 mg. That is confirmed. Calling the page 'internally inconsistent' is slightly loose. The fraction column cites refs [11]-[15] and the mass column cites Emsley [16], so these are two sources that disagree. The direction-dependent conclusion follows: at 2.17 mg the Li factor is 0.28 of P's.
(4) Potassium. 0.14 kg on the page is confirmed. stockgate.py:52 itself says the third element is '2.93x behind'. The 2.632 at :1008 is a different gap, so the audit is consistent with the tree.
(5) N and C. ICRP 110 values are confirmed from Table I. Adipose/marrow at 34.3 % of body mass with w_C 58.92 % alone contributes 20.2 points of C. That supports the audit's 'partly a different, fatter reference population' rather than a correction of ICRP 23.
(6) V, Ga, Ru, O and C rows on the page are confirmed: lines 371, 435, 451, 294 and 300. The O/C parse (45/13 kg) is supported by the atom-% check. The audit understates one point. For V and Ga, the page's independent fraction column agrees with its mass column against the tree: V 260e-9 × 70 kg = 18.2 mg against 20 mg, and Ga 4.9e-6 × 70 kg = 343 mg against 700 mg. Both differ from the tree's 0.11 mg and 0.7 mg by about 10^2 to 10^3. So the evidence leans toward the tree's two rows being transcription discrepancies, though Emsley p.83 remains unread. It still moves nothing.

NEW COMPUTED CHECK, recorded and not quoted as a refutation
Hydroxyapatite gives P/Ca = 0.4637 by mass, or 0.515 at Ca/P = 1.5. Assume, as a named hypothesis not read here, that about 99 % of the tree's 1000 g of Ca sits in bone. Then bone P is 459-510 g, and 780 g needs 270-321 g of soft-tissue P. ICRP 110's own tissue chemistry (Kanematsu, read) gives bone P/Ca 0.454 and about 90 g of soft-tissue P. That gives a total of about 545 g, which is below the 715.7 g photosphere flip. So the tree's P is high against its own Ca under ICRP 110 tissue chemistry. This corroborates the audit's sensitivity finding. It does not show ICRP 23 wrong, because ICRP 23's soft-tissue P was not read.

lacked_data
The restatement says, read verbatim, 'In 1990 in vivo data provided first estimates of body composition for Reference Woman'. It also confirms there is no Reference Woman elemental data in ICRP 23. 'Non-Western' follows from the definition's Caucasian / Western European / North American scope, so it is a scope limit rather than a demonstrated data lack.

M'S HYPOTHESIS
It is answered with evidence both ways and nothing is presumed. Later data (ICRP 89 revision, ICRP 110 tissues) exist and move which element binds. The magnitudes move by 1.2x or less, ICRP 23's table is not shown wrong, and part of the shift is a change of reference population, which is a choice of hypothesis.

GRADE
DATA-DEPENDENT is supported. STANDS is excluded because a moved datum moves the binder. WRONG is excluded because there is no counterexample to ICRP 23 itself, which remains NAMED-NOT-READ.

audits.published_statement: (4.5), p.41: K_0[phi] = Box INT_{4m^2}^inf rho(M) G^M_ret(phi) dM, with rho(M) = (1/(16 pi^2)) sqrt(1 - 4m^2/M) (1/M). (3.12)-(3.13), pp.27-28: K_0 = Box INT varrho(M)/M G_ret dM, where varrho is 'the positive-defined spectral density' (1/(16 pi^2)) sqrt(1-4m^2/M) Theta(M-4m^2). So rho = varrho/M. (4.17), p.48 (Prop 4.10): 'the Stieltjes transform of the density rho(M) given in (4.5)', J(z) := INT_{4m^2}^inf rho(M)/(M-z) dM = (1/(8 pi^2)) (1/z - (4m^2 - z) m arccsc(2m/sqrt z) / (m sqrt(4m^2 - z) z^{3/2})), z in D. Semiclassically dv/dt = F/m*, so m* < 0 inverts the acceleration response to a force, and on an inverted band the group velocity points against k. (ii) Nothing in (i) fixes the sign of the energy or of T_00. Search snippets for 2204.04041 (secondary, not a reading): 'dissipative coupling between ... excitons and photons in an optical microcavity can lead to the formation of exciton polaritons with an inverted dispersion of the lower polariton branch and hence a negative mass'; 'the propagation direction of the negative-mass polaritons is opposite to their momentum'; the samples are monolayer WS2 in planar microcavities. Snippet for 1801.04779: negative effective masses are realised 'by engineering the dispersion relation', with two effective-mass parameters (propagation and diffusion).
published_hypotheses: SEMICLASSICAL BAND MODEL (textbook, NAMED-NOT-READ): a quasiparticle wavepacket in a medium with a single-band dispersion E(k), narrow in k, under a slowly varying force. m* is then defined locally in k: a tensor in general, a scalar for an isotropic band.

2204.04041 (from snippets only): DISSIPATIVE (non-Hermitian) exciton-photon coupling in a microcavity containing a monolayer of WS2 produces the inversion. The negative mass is a property of the real part of a complex eigen-dispersion.
1801.04779 (from snippets only): negative mass by dispersion engineering in a spin-orbit-coupled BEC, with TWO effective-mass parameters (propagation and diffusion) that need not share a sign.

Measured from a band minimum, the excitation energy is >= 0 at every k whatever the sign of m* (C2, z3 UNSAT). The tree never names the reference. For the polariton the absolute energy is ~2 eV > 0, so the claim holds there. In a population-inverted medium the 'relative to the ground state' reading is not available.

verifiers.reason:
The audit graded OPEN for one reason: it could not open the source. The source opened this pass, so OPEN no longer holds. What was read at source (alphaXiv, 2026-10-02):

(1) FLAG 2411.04268v3, p.275. The held quote at massform.py:1339-1343 matches the source word for word. It leaves out the clause in front of it: "The resulting estimate for the charm quark, see, e.g., the RQCD 16 ... 70(4) MeV". So RQCD 16's 70(4) is a heavy-quark-limit ESTIMATE built from sigma_u,d,s. It is not a direct sigma_c determination, and the audit's hypothesis list ("RQCD 16 is N_f=2 ... sea content differs") misses this. The audit's phrase "the larger of the two values FLAG quotes" is also wrong. The same sentence quotes ETM 16A 79(21)(+12-8), chiQCD 13A 94(31), BMW 20A f_Tc=0.0734(45)(55) (68.9 MeV) and MILC 12C <N|cc|N>=0.056(27). 107 is still the largest of them, so the tree's "up to 107(22)" is correct.

(2) FLAG Table 3 (p.11) and Eqs. (447)/(449) (pp.272-273) confirm that FLAG forms no sigma_c average. They also confirm sigma_piN=60.9(6.5) and sigma_s=41.0(8.8). Eqs. (431)-(433) and the FLAG-def sentence (pp.260-261) are confirmed too.

(3) This is the hypothesis drift no one has named. FLAG p.267 and Table 72 (p.268) say ETM 19 comes from a single ensemble (a=0.0801 fm, M_pi=139.3 MeV), carries a red square for continuum extrapolation, and is excluded from FLAG averages. ETM 19 itself (arXiv:1909.00485v2, Table XII, p.14) confirms 107(22) MeV and f_Tc=0.115(24), from cB211.072.64 only.

(4) The datum has moved. ETM's own follow-up (arXiv:2412.01535v1, Dec 2024, Table VIII, p.11) uses three N_f=2+1+1 physical-point spacings (0.08, 0.07 and 0.06 fm). Per ensemble it gets B64 126(43), C80 43(41) and D96 80(110), and in the continuum sigma_c=82(29) MeV, from a single constant extrapolation. Its p.12 says the ETM19 results "were obtained without a continuum limit extrapolation and in addition no model averaging".

Computed: 107(22) and 82(29) differ by 0.69 combined sigma. That is a supersession, not a refutation, and nothing here is WRONG.

What survives from the audit: no tree conclusion moves. 82 MeV is below both 107 and the audit's 186 MeV threshold, so no printed figure or S10 verdict changes, and the audit's arithmetic and its drifts (uncertainty dropped, heterogeneous CONTESTED sum) stand.

Why NARROWED and not STANDS: the tree's sentence "FLAG also prints a charm sigma term, up to 107(22) MeV (ETM 19, READ)" is literally true of FLAG 2024. But 107(22) holds only under a hypothesis the tree never names: one lattice spacing and no continuum limit. FLAG flags that limitation itself, and ETM has since replaced the number with 82(29) in the continuum. The tree should name that hypothesis, and if it wants a current value, record 82(29) [2412.01535] as the newer continuum datum. That is not a repair to anything that rests on the value.

A minor point: the FLAG page-1 stamp in the served PDF reads v2 (17 Jan 2025) although alphaXiv's id is v3. The page number (p.275) matches.

What limits the result is its scope, not missing data: it rules out a Yukawa between static masses and says nothing on its own about moving branes. Applying it to a moving brane is GLP's step (2011, before Lee), and the tree takes that step over. No datum has moved since 2020 in a way that changes the conclusion. No tighter |alpha|=1 limit turned up, though one 2026 review went unread. Two agreeing verbatim restatements confirm 38.6 um. Evidence FOR a limitation, not an error: the |alpha|=1 figure is applied to an alpha = 2 potential. The right number is tighter, not looser, and switching to Lee's own 30 um changes no tree conclusion (0.22 orders, same rounding). Where the tree is actually exposed is its own use of the bound, not the measurement: it treats the upper bound on r as if it capped |c|, and it pairs r = 38.6 um with beta = 1 against its own gamma*L clause. Even so, its conclusion that the SME route gives no constraint holds at every beta GW170817 allows.

It applies the |alpha|=1 range to a compact circle whose potential, the restated GLP eq. (39), carries alpha = 2 by the computation here (alpha = 8/3 for a spin-2 KK graviton), and a larger alpha is excluded over a smaller range. Lee's own extra-dimension figure is 30 um. A dropped hypothesis means NARROWED. The effect is only that the tree's radius is too generous: every downstream figure moves by at most 0.22 orders (42.20 -> 41.98, computed), and none changes rounding, sign or verdict. O6's EOTWASH_BOUNDS clause makes no numerical claim and is untouched. Recorded, not repaired: (i) 38.6 um gives the smallest |c| over the allowed range of r; the lab bound starts to constrain below r = 3.08e-26 m at beta = 1. (ii) If K&N's form is as branelink codes it, r = 38.6 um with beta = 1 is ruled out by the tree's own gamma*L clause; the consistent bound, beta*gamma <= 1.25e21, is useless; and the conclusion still holds at GW170817's beta (57 orders below 1e-21). (2) GLP arXiv:1103.2174, eq. (39), read at source on p.14:
V_brane = -(G m1 m2/(γLr)) (1 + e^{-2πr/(γL)})/(1 - e^{-2πr/(γL)}), with L the circumference.
- On p.13 GLP say they "drop the tensor indices on the propagator to treat the graviton as a massless scalar".

- This removes the audit's conditional on GLP. The tree applies the |α| = 1 crossing to an α = 2 potential, so the gravitational-strength hypothesis H2 really was dropped.

(3) I re-ran the audit's script: it exits 0 and all checks pass. My own independent script, verify/refute/lee-check.py, reproduces every number by importing branelink directly:

(4) The audit errs in two small ways. Neither changes the grade.
- H4 and lacked_data describe "static source and detector masses". The paper says "a stationary torsion-balance detector and a rotating attractor". The masses are slowly moving, not static.
- The conditional on K&N eqs. 76-77 still stands, because I did not re-read K&N.

Refuting the grade toward STANDS fails. The rules say a dropped hypothesis is NARROWED even when the drift is conservative and every verdict survives. Here every downstream figure moves by less than 0.25 orders, with no change of sign or rounding.

Refuting it toward WRONG or DATA-DEPENDENT also fails. There is no counterexample, the number is exactly right, and no later datum that moves it was found. That last point stays conditional on the 2026 review arXiv:2605.18212, which is still unread.

The alphaXiv quota had reset by this pass, so I read the sources the audit could not open. Every data row checks out against the source. The audit's limitations were real, but none of them turned out to be wrong.

(1) value_then is right. I read Lee et al. (arXiv:2002.11761v1) at source.
